cases.abstract: Prediction-set coverage treats errors as binary, whereas segmentation and hierarchical classification require control of how much a prediction misses. Conformal risk control extends calibration to the expected value of a bounded, non-increasing loss. With n calibration observations, its rule reserves the worst-case loss B for one unseen case before selecting a parameter; monotonicity then links this conservative choice to a symmetric calibration-plus-test threshold. For exchangeable, right-continuous losses with a safe maximal parameter, this construction guarantees expected test loss at most alpha, averaging over both calibration and test data. With independent, identically distributed nonnegative losses and zero probability of a jump at any fixed parameter, the risk is also at least alpha - 2B/(n+1); this worst-case gap is sharp. Boundedness alone is insufficient: non-monotone losses can drive risk arbitrarily close to B. Across segmentation, multilabel classification, hierarchical classification, and question answering, 1,000 random splits per task yield mean risks near their targets. Extensions cover additional risk functionals and specified shifts, but do not remove the need for monotonicity or information about non-exchangeability.
cases.methods: Given n calibration losses, let R_n(lambda) denote their mean and B an upper bound on each loss. Choose the smallest lambda satisfying [n R_n(lambda) + B]/(n+1) <= alpha, falling back to the maximal parameter whose loss is at most alpha if none qualifies. Reserving B for the unseen case makes this corrected average an upper bound on the average of all n+1 losses. The proof compares the chosen parameter with an infeasible threshold calibrated on that complete sample. The observable choice is no smaller, so monotonicity makes its test loss no larger. Conditional on the unordered sample, exchangeability makes the held-out loss at the symmetric threshold average to the full-sample mean. Right-continuity ensures that this threshold meets the risk constraint. Thus, the correction transfers a full-sample inequality to expected test loss averaged over calibration and test randomness.
cases.results: On hierarchical ImageNet, mean normalized distance loss is 0.0499 (between-split standard deviation 0.0011) at alpha = 0.05, yet predictions are almost always leaf nodes. Thus, control in this example is not achieved simply by always choosing coarse ancestors. At alpha = 0.1, polyp segmentation and MS COCO yield mean false-negative losses of 0.0987 and 0.0996, with between-split standard deviations of 0.0114 and 0.0052, respectively, across 1,000 random splits each. These results support near-target average risk, not control within every split or a count of wholly correct prediction sets. Calibration sizes differ (1,000 versus 4,000), so the dispersion contrast does not isolate an application effect. The non-monotone counterexample exposes the structural boundary: the same calibration rule can yield expected loss arbitrarily close to B. Taking each loss's supremum over larger parameter values restores monotonicity and control, but can become conservative when the original loss is far from monotone.
cases.notes: Preserved expected-risk control and its tight lower bound as distinct contributions (Theorems 1-2; Proposition 1). The abstract links the unseen-loss reserve to the symmetric comparison explained in Methods. Results connect hierarchical resolution to risk (Section 3.3), retain between-split standard deviations (Sections 3.1-3.3), and use Proposition 2 and Corollary 1 to delimit the non-monotone case. The question-answering threshold direction is not reproduced. Shift extensions are not presented as protection against unknown drift.

cases.abstract: Refitting a predictor and updating its score quantiles does not ensure coverage when the score distribution drifts. Adaptive conformal inference addresses the remaining mismatch by adjusting the quantile level after each revealed outcome, increasing it after a miss and decreasing it after coverage. With a fixed positive step size and quantile conventions permitting full or empty prediction sets, the update guarantees convergence of realized miscoverage frequency to the target for any data-generating sequence. This long-run frequency guarantee does not establish coverage at every time. Under stationary hidden Markov assumptions, fixed score and quantile functions, and additional regularity conditions, stronger bounds connect concentration and mean squared marginal miscoverage error to environmental dependence and changes in the optimal calibration parameter. Volatility forecasting and county-level election examples illustrate local coverage closer to the 90% target than fixed nominal calibration, including when volatility forecasts are refitted on recent data. Removing volatility normalization nevertheless produces wider coverage swings despite adaptation. Feedback therefore complements score design rather than replacing it, and the method requires responses to be revealed at each step.
cases.methods: For target miscoverage alpha, threshold the current score at its estimated quantile Q_t(1-alpha_t). Once the response is revealed, set err_t to one for a miss and zero otherwise, then update alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma(alpha-err_t). A miss raises the requested quantile level, enlarging the set when the score and quantile functions are held fixed. For gamma > 0 and alpha_1 in [0,1], conventions producing full sets when alpha_t < 0 and empty sets when alpha_t > 1 keep alpha_t in [-gamma,1+gamma] without clipping. Summing the recursion gives (1/T) sum_{t=1}^T err_t - alpha = (alpha_1-alpha_{T+1})/(gamma T). The absolute frequency deviation is therefore at most [max{alpha_1,1-alpha_1}+gamma]/(gamma T), irrespective of the data-generating sequence. The guarantee follows from bounded feedback, not a distributional model, and concerns accumulated errors rather than marginal coverage at every time.
cases.results: In volatility forecasting, adaptive calibration keeps 500-day local coverage near 90%, whereas fixed nominal calibration departs markedly, including undercoverage for Fannie Mae during the 2008 crisis. Both procedures refit GARCH forecasts and calibrate scores using 1,250 trading days, so the contrast tests feedback beyond recent-data refitting. The four plotted stocks were selected for conspicuous fixed-calibration failures among twelve examined; favorable adaptive performance across all twelve is reported. Replacing volatility-normalized residuals with absolute residuals produces much wider coverage swings even with feedback. Adaptation therefore does not eliminate sensitivity to score drift. In the election example, adaptive calibration maintains approximately 90% local coverage over 300-county windows, while fixed calibration dips at time-zone transitions. Counties are ordered by time zone and randomized within zones rather than by actual reporting times. The comparison supports adaptation to the constructed geographic drift, not a reconstruction of election-night performance.
cases.notes: Proposition 4.1 anchors the telescoping argument and cumulative-frequency claim. Theorems 4.1-4.2 require stationarity of the joint environment-parameter process, fixed score and quantile functions, and further spectral-gap or Lipschitz conditions; these do not automatically cover rolling refits. The abstract's feedback-versus-score-design interpretation is anchored by Sections 2.2 and 5. Results preserve the selected-stock display and constructed time-zone ordering (Sections 2.2 and 6). Local windows are described by length without calling the centered stock evaluation window trailing. No interval-width improvement is claimed.
